text: The question arrives before the diploma does: marry now, or finish school. Yuni is the student who wants the second answer, and Kamila Andini spends the film on the cost of saying so out loud in a place where the first answer is simply assumed. Ninety-five minutes, in Indonesian, a French production sent out as an international submission to the Academy Awards. What gives it its charge is that there is no villain in it. The expectation is ambient: it comes from women who were once girls with plans, from teachers who mean well, from the arithmetic of a household that has already counted her. Against that, a final-year student has her own stubbornness and whatever time remains in the school year, and the film is honest about how short both are.

The affair is over before the film begins; what the couple has to live with is everything it left standing. Nanouk Leopold takes a psychiatrist — a woman whose working day is built out of other people's disclosures — and gives her a private history she cannot account for, professionally or otherwise, then moves her, her husband and the whole unspoken arrangement to India. The relocation changes the light and the language and nothing else. Ninety-seven minutes, in English, out of Germany, and closer to a study than a story: rooms held a beat past comfort, exchanges that stop just short of the sentence they exist to produce. The question underneath is how two people go on sharing a house after one of them has been unknowable inside it. Leopold keeps her distance from both, and the distance does the work.

Two hours and twelve minutes is a long time to give competitive cup stacking, and that excess is the design. Nawapol Thamrongrattanarit hands his hero a world title in a sport measured in hundredths of a second, then removes the girlfriend who has evidently been running everything else, and watches a man who can move his hands faster than anyone alive fail to manage one ordinary day alone. The film crossbreeds its genres on purpose: training montage against domestic argument, action grammar applied to chores, romance conducted in the vocabulary of records and personal bests. Thai, 2022, and patient with its own jokes. Speed is what he is good at and the one thing that cannot help him, since the skills he lacks are the slow kind, learned by repetition and not against a clock.

Summer 2010 in Tunis, a few months before the revolution, and the songs Farah sings with her band are already the kind that get noticed. She is eighteen and freshly graduated; her family has settled on medicine for her. Leyla Bouzid builds the film out of two kinds of knowledge — a girl learning her own city after dark, and her mother Hayet, who learned it earlier and by harder means. The music carries the argument: rehearsals, the volume of a voice in a small room, the difference between a lyric on paper and a lyric sung to strangers. The coming upheaval stays offscreen and presses on everything, mostly as the wariness of everyone older than her. It won a Bayard d'or. Ninety-eight minutes, much of it at night.

Yanji in winter, a city on China's northern border where the cold is the main civic fact. Anthony Chen drops three people into it: a young man visiting from Shanghai with no clear idea what he is doing there, the tour guide who shows him around, and her friend, a restaurant worker whose frustration sits close to the surface. They spend a drunken weekend together. That is nearly the whole plot, which frees the film for something harder to summarize — the weight of being young in a place nobody chose, in a season that shortens the day and lengthens everything else. A hundred minutes, shot close. All three know the arrangement is temporary, and that knowledge is what lets them say things they would never say to someone staying.

Two men are pulling in opposite directions and both of them are hers: a younger boyfriend sinking into drugs, and a grown son who has walked away from the army. The woman between them is transgender, Portuguese, and unwilling to give up either. João Pedro Rodrigues gives this a hundred and thirty-three minutes and threads music through it, which lifts what could have been a case history into melodrama in the older sense, where feeling is a form rather than a lapse. Care is the real subject: who is assumed to owe it, who performs it, what it costs a person who has already spent years assembling herself against opposition. Portugal sent the film out as its international submission to the Academy Awards. Nothing in it is arranged to reassure, least of all the tenderness.

One of the two studies mosses for a living; the other works on Brussels building sites. Bas Devos gives their meeting eighty-four minutes, which sounds slight and is exactly right: a bryologist's attention requires kneeling on wet ground and waiting, and the film adopts that posture toward its own city. Scale is the whole argument — excavation and cranes on one side, green things surviving in pavement cracks on the other, two adults moving between them at the speed of strangers being polite. The romance, if that is what it becomes, is made of small courtesies and long pauses. Devos will hold on weather, on plants, on silences other films would trim, and the effect is that a European capital starts to look like a habitat with residents nobody counted.

The seduction runs through a reading list. Ahmed is eighteen, French and Algerian, raised on the outskirts of Paris, and at university he discovers that classical Arabic literature holds centuries of frank erotic writing nobody had mentioned to him — in the same term that he meets Farah, just arrived from Tunis and unembarrassed by any of it. Leyla Bouzid makes his restraint the plot. He is fluent in his inheritance only by halves, and the woman teaching him the rest of it is the one he is too proud, or too frightened, to touch. A hundred and two minutes, moving between a campus and a suburb. Desire is treated as something with a history and a bibliography, which turns hesitation into an event rather than a delay in one.

An eighteen-year-old volunteers with ideas about heroism assembled from somewhere other than experience, and is shipped to Libya. Václav Marhoul follows Czechoslovak soldiers fighting the Germans at Tobruk, and treats the desert as the primary antagonist: sand, heat, exposure, and the ubiquity of a death not attached to any particular engagement. Jiri Pospichal is the young one. Jan is there too, and a good deal of the strain runs between men on the same side, in a unit small enough that nobody can be avoided for long. Ninety-nine minutes, in Czech. What Marhoul keeps returning to is the distance between the words a boy uses about war before he arrives and the ones left available to him afterwards.

Inside a mechanical watch one wheel swings back and forth and never settles; in a nineteenth-century Swiss factory town, a woman named Josephine is paid to make them. Cyril Schäublin builds a film out of that job and the arguments going on beside it: how a working day is measured, whose time the town runs on, what a wage means when the same hour can be counted four different ways. Anarchists are organizing in the valley. So are the people who own the machines. Nothing is scaled up to revolution — it is benches, ledgers, timetables, the setting of a public clock, new technology arriving as paperwork before it arrives as anything else. Ninety-four minutes, in German, dry and level, and finally about the one thing a factory truly manufactures, which is the shape of a day.

A university professor is shot in the street with his daughter next to him, and the police give her nothing to hold. Paula studies art. She has no training for what she does instead, which is to go looking for the man herself, in a city where the difficulty may not turn out to be the finding. Laura Mora Ortega keeps this at street level and refuses the machinery of a thriller: no procedure, no evidence board, only a young woman asking questions that put her family in the same position as herself. The pressure is moral rather than investigative — grief acquires a plan very quickly, and the plan requires proximity. A hundred minutes, in Spanish. Anger is easy to photograph; what Mora is after is the point at which it hardens into a decision.

The script came out of a stranger's tweets. Nawapol Thamrongrattanarit built the film from posts by an anonymous Thai girl, and it advances the way a timeline does: by jump, by joke, by something serious dropped without warning between two trivialities. Mary is in her final year of school, and the year's ordinary business is all present — a friendship under strain, love, the low panic of what comes after. The method could have been a stunt. It holds for a hundred and twenty-seven minutes because adolescence really is discontinuous, and a structure with no transitions turns out to be the honest one. The comedy is deadpan, the images are odder than the premise promises, and Nawapol will let a strange thing stand in the frame without explaining it.

A girl's body starts doing something the school has no procedure for. Amanda Nell Eu sets this in an all-girls school, in Malay, and lets the horror genre take literally what the adults are already treating as contamination. The premise is old — puberty as monstrosity — and the handling is not: the pressure comes less from teachers than from other students, from the speed at which a rumour hardens into a fact about a person. Ninety-five minutes, a French production, sent out as an international submission to the Academy Awards. Eu keeps the ordinary comedy of schoolgirls running underneath the dread, so the film never quite settles into being frightening; it slides back into playground noise, which is where the cruelty lives anyway.
